title: The quotation と, compound verbs and nouns
summary: と closes whatever came before it into a single quoted unit. Verbs and nouns can also be glued together to make new words.

blocks.text: This lesson continues the cat's story from lesson 11. It covers two words for "thing", the quotation と that wraps up speech and thought, and two ways of gluing words together: compound verbs and compound nouns.
Two words for "thing". **もの** is a concrete object (a hat, a book, a mountain). **こと** is an abstract matter or circumstance: something that happens or is the case.

blocks.en: Is there something (a thing) in the box?
Nothing interesting is happening. (no interesting matter exists)

blocks.text: This と is a different particle from the "and" と. It works like a spoken quotation mark. It follows speech or thought, usually with **言う** (say) or **思う** (think). Whatever comes before it, a single word or an entire clause with its own grammar, is wrapped up into one unit, and that unit describes the verb after it.
「遅い！」と言った。 The quote is one white car.

blocks.jp: 猫は「面白いことがない」と言った。
blocks.en: The cat said, "Nothing interesting is happening."

blocks.text: The one who speaks can be shared with the first clause: the same cat who sees, says and then runs.

blocks.jp: 兄は「遅い！」と言って、走り出した。
blocks.en: My brother said "I'm late!" and burst into a run.

blocks.text: The same idea carries to sounds and manner: ぴょんぴょんと is a hopping "quote" that describes how someone moves. にこにこと (smiling) works the same way.

blocks.jp: うさぎはぴょんぴょんと走り続けた。
blocks.en: The rabbit kept running, hopping along.

blocks.text: Another small tip: そのとき ("at that time") works like a relative time word, so it takes no に.
Stick the **い-stem** of one verb onto another verb and you get a new meaning. 出す adds "suddenly begin", 続ける adds "keep doing", 過ぎる adds "pass", and 込む adds "into, with force".
走り出す = run + begin suddenly.

blocks.jp: バスが家の前を通り過ぎた。
blocks.en: The bus passed by the house.
The cat jumped into the hole.

blocks.text: Two nouns can simply be placed side by side, with no の. The first sound of the second noun often turns voiced (a **か** becomes **が**, a **そ** becomes **ぞ**, a **と** becomes **ど**). This is called 連濁. As a rough rule it happens often with native (kun) readings: 青 + 空 = 青空, 懐中 + 時計 = 懐中時計.
Watch out for look-alike words: 読んだ (read) and 呼んだ (called) both look the same in kana, よんだ. Context tells you which one it is.
A て-form plus **ください** is a polite request, and ください can be dropped: ちょっと待って(ください). The word comes from くれる in lesson 11: ください means "please give down to me", so 待ってください is "give me the waiting".

blocks.jp: ちょっと待ってください。

blocks.title: Remember
items: **もの** = concrete thing; **こと** = abstract matter.
**…と言う / 思う**: と wraps what comes before it into a quote.
Compound verb: **い-stem + another verb** (走り出す, 飛び込む).
Compound noun: two nouns side by side, the second often voiced (**青空**).
